per_option_rationale.rationale: Converting 27^(-1) to 3^(-1) instead of 3^(-3) (misidentifying 27 as 3^1). Numerator becomes 3^3 x 3^(-1) = 3^2 = 9. Divided by 3^2: 9/9 = 1. Then student re-examines and arrives at 3^(-1) = 1/3 by one further step error.

Student applies the denominator 3^2 as a multiplier to the exponent of 27^(-1) instead of dividing by it: computes 3^3 x 3^(-3+2) = 3^3 x 3^(-1) = 3^2... or simplifies 3^0/3^2 incorrectly as 3^(2-0) = 3^2/3^3 = 3^(-1), then flips to get 3^1 = 3.
Student drops the negative sign on 27^(-1), treating it as 27^1. Then numerator = 3^3 x 3^3 = 3^6 = 729. Divided by 3^2 = 9: 729/9 = 81.

explanation_sections.punchline: Expressing 9 and 27 as powers of 3 reduces every factor to the same base, making exponent arithmetic straightforward.
explanation_sections.approach: Indices simplification: identify the common base (3). Convert: 9 = 3^2, 27 = 3^3. Apply power-of-a-power rule: 9^(3/2) = 3^3; 27^(-1) = 3^(-3). Numerator: 3^3 x 3^(-3) = 3^0 = 1. Denominator: 3^2 = 9. Final result: 1/9.
explanation_sections.lesson: Convert all bases to their prime form first, then add exponents for multiplication and subtract for division. A negative exponent on 27 must be applied to the full power 3^3, giving 3^(-3), not 3^(-1).
explanation_sections.timing: 60 seconds. Trap: dropping the negative exponent on 27^(-1) and computing 81.
